title: Encrypt and Decrypt Strings
statement:
Build a class `Encrypter` that turns words into a two-letter code and back. The constructor receives `keys` (distinct lowercase characters), `values` (lowercase strings of length 2, where `values[i]` is the code of `keys[i]`; several keys may share one code) and `dictionary`, a list of distinct words that count as valid plain text.

- `encrypt(word1)` replaces each character of `word1`, left to right, by its code and returns the joined result. If a character had no code the answer would be `""`, but every character of `word1` is guaranteed to be one of `keys`.
- `decrypt(word2)` splits `word2` into consecutive blocks of 2 letters starting at index 0 and may replace each block by any key whose code equals that block. Since a code can belong to several keys or to none, `word2` can decode to many different strings or to none. Return how many of those possible strings are words of `dictionary`.
constraints: All keys[i] are distinct, and all dictionary[i] are distinct
Every character of word1 appears in keys
keys, values[i], dictionary[i], word1 and word2 contain only lowercase English letters
At most 200 calls are made to encrypt and decrypt in total

signature.name: Encrypter
signature.constructor: Encrypter(char[] keys, String[] values, String[] dictionary)

notes:
## Intuition

Decoding `word2` directly means choosing a key for every 2-letter block. When codes are shared those choices multiply: 100 blocks with two candidates each give 2^100 strings, far too many to list. Turn the question around. Encryption is deterministic, so a dictionary word `d` is a possible decoding of `word2` exactly when `encrypt(d) === word2`. Because the dictionary is fixed and its words are distinct, we can encrypt every word once in the constructor and count how many words produce each coded string. Each `decrypt` is then a single map lookup.

## Approach

1. In the constructor, fill `codeOf` so that each key maps to its 2-letter code.
2. Encrypt every dictionary `word`. A word that uses a letter outside `keys` encrypts to `""` and can never be decoded, so skip it.
3. Count the coded strings in `countOf`: `countOf[encrypted]` is how many dictionary words encrypt to `encrypted`.
4. `encrypt(word1)` looks up each character's `code`, collects the codes in `parts` and joins them (or returns `""` for an unknown character).
5. `decrypt(word2)` returns `countOf.get(word2)`, or 0 when no dictionary word encrypts to it.

## Example 1, step by step

`a` and `c` both have code `ei`, `b` has `zf`, `d` has `am`. Encrypting the dictionary gives `abcd -> eizfeiam`, `acbd -> eieizfam`, `adbc -> eiamzfei`, `badc -> zfeiamei`, `dacb -> ameieizf`, `cadb -> eieiamzf`, `cbda -> eizfamei` and `abad -> eizfeiam`, so `countOf` holds `eizfeiam` with count 2 and the others with count 1. `encrypt("abcd")` joins `ei`, `zf`, `ei`, `am` into `"eizfeiam"`, and `decrypt("eizfeiam")` reads its count, `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: the constructor is O(D·L) for D dictionary words of length up to L; `encrypt` is O(|word1|); `decrypt` is O(|word2|) for hashing the string.
- Space: O(D·L) for the encrypted dictionary.

## Pitfalls

- Do not enumerate every decoding; shared codes make their number exponential.
- Blocks start at even indices only: `"xxaa"` contains `"xa"` at index 1, but that is not a block.
- Dictionary words with a letter missing from `keys` must not be counted under the empty string.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `codeOf` | key character -> its 2-letter code |
| `countOf` | coded string -> how many dictionary words encrypt to it |
| `encrypted` | the coded form of one dictionary word |
| `parts` | the codes collected while encrypting |
| `code` | the code of the current character |

narration.3: codeOf will map each key character to its 2-letter code.
narration.5: Record that keys[i] is written as values[i].
narration.7: countOf will map a coded string to how many dictionary words encrypt to it.
narration.8: Encrypt every allowed word once, up front, so decrypt never has to search.
narration.10: A word with a letter outside keys cannot be produced by decrypting, so it is skipped.
narration.13: Count one more dictionary word behind this coded string.
narration.19: Encrypt left to right, one character at a time.
narration.22: An unknown character makes encryption impossible, so the result is the empty string.
narration.26: Glue the codes together in order.
narration.30: A dictionary word decodes from word2 exactly when it encrypts to word2, so the stored count is the answer.
